chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Yazid ibn Ishaq Sha'ir, who raised it to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a female slave manumitted from behind (from one side of her master's ownership) by her master. He said: Whatever she bears, they are in her position, and they are from his third. If they are more than the third, they are made to bear the deficiency. And the manumission (kitabah) is for whatever she bears during her manumission period; they are in her position. If she dies, then upon them is what remains of her debt, if they wish. So when they pay it, they are manumitted.

key_terms.أُعْتِقَتْ مِنْ دُبُرٍ: Manumitted from behind (a slave owned by one master who owns half of her, or similar partial ownership structure)
key_terms.اسْتُسْعُوا: They were made to bear/cover (the deficiency)
key_terms.الْمُكَاتَبَةُ: Manumission contract (kitabah) where a slave pays a fixed sum for freedom
key_terms.ثُلُث: Third (referring to the share of the estate or debt)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for the children of a female slave who is manumitted from behind?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani’s al-Ishtibār clarifies the fiqh of the *umm al-walad* (mother of a child) whose manumission is deferred until her master’s death, specifically addressing the legal status of her offspring born during the interim period. It establishes that these children inherit her partial freedom and are liable for the remaining manumission debt (*kitabah*) from the master’s estate, ensuring their eventual full emancipation. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on the automatic elevation of status for children born to a partially freed slave, balancing the master’s financial rights with the slaves' path to liberty.
